approachQuestion.prompt:
Shared Booking Windows

Two read-only lists first and second contain closed integer intervals [start,end], with start<=end. In each list, intervals are sorted by start and strictly separated: the end of an interval is less than the start of the next interval. Return their shared windows: every nonempty intersection between an interval from first and an interval from second, in increasing start order. A singleton [t,t] is a nonempty shared window.

Constraints: 0 <= n=first.length, m=second.length <= 200000; endpoints are in [-1000000000,1000000000]. Return a new list of intervals; do not mutate either input.

Example 1: first=[[1,4],[8,10]], second=[[3,8]] -> [[3,4],[8,8]].
Example 2: first=[[1,2]], second=[[3,5]] -> [].
Example 3: first=[], second=[[1,1]] -> [].
constraints: Choose the most efficient valid approach for the entire stated input domain; accept equivalent optimal variants.

options.text: Compare current intervals. Emit [max(starts),min(ends)] if its start does not exceed its end. Advance the interval with smaller end; advance both on equal ends. Stop when either list ends.
options.feedback: An interval ending first cannot overlap a future interval in the other separated list. The longer current interval remains available for further overlaps.

options.text: Copy both interval lists, then run the same earlier-end sweep on those copies.
options.feedback: The sweep is correct but only reads intervals, so copying them adds unnecessary storage and work.

options.text: Compare current intervals and emit a nonempty intersection, then always advance both lists.
options.feedback: For first=[[1,4],[8,10]], second=[[3,8]], this emits [3,4] and misses [8,8].

options.text: Use the earlier-end sweep but emit an intersection only when max(starts)<min(ends).
options.feedback: For first=[[1,2]], second=[[2,3]], it misses the required singleton [2,2].

feedback.reason: Advance the interval that expires first, with explicit closed-endpoint semantics and protection against skipping one-to-many overlaps.
details: At the current interval pair, take the larger start and smaller end. Append that interval when start<=end. Then consume whichever input interval ends earlier; if the ends are equal, consume both. Continue while both inputs have an interval.

The overlap uses max(starts) and min(ends). Inclusive endpoints make a single shared endpoint a valid overlap. Advancing the earlier-ending interval is safe because it cannot overlap a future interval beyond its end.

“Compare current intervals. Emit [max(starts),min(ends)] if its start does not exceed its end. Advance the interval with smaller end; advance both on equal ends. Stop when either list ends.”: An interval ending first cannot overlap a future interval in the other separated list. The longer current interval remains available for further overlaps.
“Copy both interval lists, then run the same earlier-end sweep on those copies.”: The sweep is correct but only reads intervals, so copying them adds unnecessary storage and work.
“Compare current intervals and emit a nonempty intersection, then always advance both lists.”: For first=[[1,4],[8,10]], second=[[3,8]], this emits [3,4] and misses [8,8].
“Use the earlier-end sweep but emit an intersection only when max(starts)<min(ends).”: For first=[[1,2]], second=[[2,3]], it misses the required singleton [2,2].

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the fixed method revealed after question 1, choose its tight worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. Use a word-RAM model with constant-time indexed access and signed 64-bit arithmetic. Include all temporary buffers, input copies, and call frames; exclude supplied input and returned output. n and m are the list lengths. Output append is amortized constant time and output-list resizing/copying is included in time and treated as output storage. The method is iterative; no input copies, auxiliary interval lists, recursion, or hashing.
constraints: Analyze this fixed method regardless of your answer to question 1; choose the tightest pair.

options.text: O(n + m + 1) time, O(1) auxiliary space
O(n + m + 1) time, O(n + m + 1) auxiliary space
O((n + m + 1) log(n + m + 2)) time, O(1) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Each iteration consumes at least one interval from the input lists.
details: Each iteration consumes at least one input interval, so there are at most n+m iterations and at most that many output windows. Interleaved lists force linear work. Excluding the returned interval list, only indices and endpoint scalars are retained.

Use a word-RAM model with constant-time indexed access and signed 64-bit arithmetic. Include all temporary buffers, input copies, and call frames; exclude supplied input and returned output. n and m are the list lengths. Output append is amortized constant time and output-list resizing/copying is included in time and treated as output storage. The method is iterative; no input copies, auxiliary interval lists, recursion, or hashing.
“O(n + m + 1) time, O(n + m + 1) auxiliary space”: This adds copied interval lists absent from the fixed method.
“O((n + 1)(m + 1)) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The sweep does not compare every cross-list interval pair.
“O((n + m + 1) log(n + m + 2)) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Both lists are already sorted and no sorting occurs.
